Report: Double Fine's union drive collapsed due to miscommunication and culture clash
It appears the question of union eligibility crashed headlong into Double Fine Productions' decades-old company culture.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
October 9, 2026
schedule
4 Min Read
Image via Double Fine Productions
In May 2026, employees at Double Fine Productions—then a subsidiary of Microsoft—filed
a petition to unionize
. It seemed at the time to be the latest in a string of union petitions that proved successful at sibling organizations like
Blizzard Entertainment
,
ZeniMax
, and other Xbox-owned game studios. But a new report from Kotaku shows that from the moment union organizers stepped into the spotlight, they became embroiled in a studio-wide conflict that ended with them withdrawing their petition.
That union drive was apparently the second one to take place at Double Fine, as another had begun to pick up steam in 2019 after studio founder and CEO Tim Schaefer delivered an affirming comedy set celebrating unions at GDC 2019. That drive was stymied in part by the COVID-19 pandemic.
What drove the conflict? Unfortunately, as Kotaku's report lays out, it seems to be a clash between Double Fine's loose organizational culture and the eligibility requirements for unionization as determined under US federal law. This led some employees to allegedly cut off communications with their coworkers and fueled a number of antagonistic interactions between union supporters and employees who felt Double Fine "didn't need" a union.
Related:
Trump administration suspends Microsoft's ability to apply for green cards, alleging fraud
The question of eligibility proved thorny because under US law, managers with hiring and firing power are unable to join unions. But Double Fine's flat organizational structure meant many employees had at one point or another, been managers. Attempts to clear up this confusion were hampered by some workers' prediction that unionization would destroy Double Fine's unique work culture. All this took place under the shadow of what is known inside Double Fine as "The Bad Meeting," an event documented in the 2023 documentary
Double Fine PsychOdyssey
, where a group discussion over potential crunch turned heated.
Sources told Kotaku that some employees that the meeting was even more hostile than what was portrayed onscreen, and was emblematic of a reported social divide in Double Fine's work culture. This hostility apparently surfaced again in the union drive, with one unidentified employee (who was eligible to join the union) reportedly voicing their opposition loudly and publicly in the workplace, at one point "yelling at" a colleague over the union and "bringing them to tears."
Studio founder and CEO Tim Schaefer acknowledged this conflict in an hour-long interview with Kotaku, which you can read
the full transcript of here
. When pressed about why he or other leaders didn't intervene as arguments between employees apparently escalated, he stressed his desire to stay uninvolved in unionization conversations due to his role as CEO.
Related:
Denuvo attempts to subpoena Discord, Valve, and Reddit in effort to identify hacker
"I felt like I couldn’t interfere between eligible employees talking," he told Kotaku. When pressed about why the eight union organizers at Double Fine were among
the 23 employees laid off in July 2026
, he denied any link between the failed union drive and that decision.
"That’s definitely not the reason," he said. "We didn’t target people for layoffs." He intimated that the company's priority was to retain "who we most desperately need to make these games." The laid-off workers told Kotaku they did receive a generous severance package. "I thought it was important to match Microsoft," said the CEO.
The full tale—which you should
take time to read in its entirety
—paints a picture of what happens when sincere questions about union regulations collide with individuals who appear willing to escalate those concerns into interpersonal conflict.
"The conversations just made me feel astounded at the immense dysfunction I was seeing," said one manager who hadn't been eligible to join the union. Another ineligible worker told the outlet that they witnessed pro-union employees do their best to answer questions about procedures and eligibility in non-official channels, while anti-union workers (both eligible and ineligible) fought against the effort in company channels.
Related:

"Seeing how quickly people who supported unions in other companies turned against their colleagues who are pro-union made me think that a union was very much needed at Double Fine" this individual said. "It was clear that those anti-union people in no way would have the back of their colleagues if anything bad happened and it became an us-versus-them situation."
